text:
Jane (ECorp): Hey team — after a firewall change yesterday our Redwood Private cluster mTLS connections to the control plane started failing intermittently. Clients get TLS handshake failures and our app logs show repeated ClientHello retransmits. Can someone help triage?

Alex K.: Sorry to hear that. Do you have a packet capture or openssl s_client output? Also which control plane hostname/IP are you hitting and from which AZ/VPC?

Jane (ECorp): We hit control-plane.ecorp.redwood.example:443 from a VPC in us-east-1 (NAT + Azure ExpressRoute). Sample openssl output below — it completes handshake sometimes but most attempts fail with no server response: 

```
$ openssl s_client -connect control-plane.ecorp.redwood.example:443 -cert client.pem -key client.key -state -debug
CONNECTED(00000003)
139837... wait...
---
no peer certificate available
---
SSL handshake has read 0 bytes and written 345 bytes
---
read:errno=104
```

Jane (ECorp): tcpdump snippet from our customer gateway (trimmed):

```
12:34:01.123456 IP 10.0.0.5.49156 > 3.122.45.67.443: Flags [S], seq 12345, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 123 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0
12:34:01.123789 IP 10.0.0.5.49156 > 3.122.45.67.443: Flags [S], seq 12345, length 0 (retransmission)
12:34:02.223456 IP 10.0.0.5.49156 > 3.122.45.67.443: Flags [S], seq 12345, length 0 (retransmission)
12:34:02.223789 IP 10.0.0.5.49156 > 3.122.45.67.443: Flags [R], seq 0, length 0
```

Maya R.: That looks like the outside peer is not responding to the SYN or there's a NAT/firewall dropping the return path. Two quick things to check: 1) egress allowlist / NSG rules — make sure ephemeral port range outbound is allowed (49152-65535 by default) and return traffic isn't blocked. 2) ipset or firewall rules that match the control-plane IPs and drop mid-handshake.

Raj (NetOps): We had an ipset rule rolled yesterday to block a botnet range — it accidentally used a CIDR that overlapped one of Redwood's control plane IPs. I'm pulling the nslookup logs now.

Alex K.: If you can, run these from a failing host and paste outputs: 

```
# DNS resolution
dig +short control-plane.ecorp.redwood.example

# Trace open conn and TLS
curl -v --cert client.pem --key client.key https://control-plane.ecorp.redwood.example/health || true

# OpenSSL with SNI and client certs
openssl s_client -connect control-plane.ecorp.redwood.example:443 -servername control-plane.ecorp.redwood.example -cert client.pem -key client.key -msg -debug
```

Jane (ECorp): dig returns 3.122.45.67. curl shows connection reset on read. I ran a quick iptables-save on the gateway, nothing obvious. Raj — any update on ipset?

Raj (NetOps): Confirmed — ipset 'blocklist-quick' included 3.122.45.64/29 due to a mistaken script. I removed the entry at 12:30 UTC. Can you re-run the capture?

Jane (ECorp): Re-ran capture after removal — looks stable now, no retransmits, TLS handshake completes every time. Thanks.

Maya R.: Glad that was it. For long-term: 1) pin Redwood control plane IPs in the allowlist (we can provide the full CIDR set), 2) prefer DNS-based allowlist with monitoring alerts for DNS changes, and 3) avoid broad ipset drops that include small control-plane blocks — use explicit CIDRs and change-review.

Alex K.: I'll open an internal note to publish the control-plane IP ranges and add a short runbook for customers: recommended egress ports (443), ephemeral port requirements (outbound uses ephemeral source ports 49152-65535), and recommended NSG/ipset patterns.

Support Bot: Escalation SR-78921 created and linked to internal ticket RDW-9853.

Jane (ECorp): Thanks everyone — please share the IP/CIDR list and we'll confirm our allowlists. :thumbsup:
